title: Wrist osteoarthritis and frailty: choosing a walking aid that does not hurt (UK)

content:
Walking aids can help you stay steady, but they put weight through your hands and wrists. With wrist osteoarthritis, this can be painful.

This guide explains options to discuss with a professional. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why wrists hurt with walking aids

  • Weight goes through the wrist at an angle.
  • Gripping a thin handle needs strong grip.
  • An aid at the wrong height increases strain.

Options that may help

  • Shaped or padded handles that spread pressure.
  • Forearm support frames or gutter frames that take weight through the forearm.
  • Wheeled walkers that need less lifting.
  • Making sure the height is correct.

Getting assessed

A physiotherapist or occupational therapist can assess which aid suits you and check the height. Ask your GP for a referral. Many aids are loaned free through community equipment services.

Caring for your wrists

Splints may help some people. Pain relief and hand exercises can be discussed with your GP or physiotherapist.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Should I stop using my stick if my wrist hurts?

Not without advice. Ask for an assessment for a different aid.

Can I buy my own walking aid?

You can, but an assessment helps ensure it is right for you.
